taxonomy.subsystem: Central and peripheral nervous system tumors
taxonomy.subtopic: Bilateral cerebellopontine-angle tumors and NF2/merlin loss

questions.stem_html: A 24-year-old woman has gradually progressive hearing loss in both ears, intermittent tinnitus, and unsteadiness when walking in the dark. Magnetic resonance imaging shows enhancing masses at both cerebellopontine angles extending into the internal auditory canals, as depicted in the accompanying schematic. Loss of which protein function most directly predisposed this patient to these tumors?

options.text_html: Merlin-mediated tumor suppression at the cell cortex and growth-signaling interfaces
Neurofibromin-mediated acceleration of RAS GTP hydrolysis
VHL-mediated recognition of hydroxylated hypoxia-inducible factor
APC-mediated degradation of beta-catenin
Tuberin-mediated inhibition of RHEB and mTOR signaling

questions.explanation_html: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas in a young adult strongly indicate NF2-related schwannomatosis. The NF2 gene on chromosome 22 encodes merlin, a tumor-suppressor protein that links membrane-cytoskeletal organization with growth-control pathways. Germline loss of one NF2 allele followed by somatic loss of the second permits Schwann-cell proliferation and also predisposes to meningiomas and ependymomas.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Neurofibromin is encoded by NF1 and downregulates RAS; NF1 is associated with neurofibromas, optic pathway gliomas, and other findings rather than bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: VHL protein targets hydroxylated HIF for degradation; VHL loss predisposes to clear-cell renal cell carcinoma and hemangioblastomas.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: APC participates in beta-catenin degradation and is classically altered in familial adenomatous polyposis.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Tuberin is encoded by TSC2 and restrains mTOR signaling; its loss causes tuberous sclerosis complex.

questions.educational_objective: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark of NF2-related schwannomatosis, which results from loss of the merlin tumor suppressor encoded by NF2 on chromosome 22.

media.alt_text: Original schematic axial MRI showing bilateral cerebellopontine-angle masses extending into the internal auditory canals.

questions.stem_html: A 33-year-old woman has dry cough, anterior uveitis, and fatigue. Chest imaging shows symmetric bilateral hilar lymph-node enlargement, and a transbronchial biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas. Laboratory studies reveal calcium of 11.4 mg/dL, suppressed parathyroid hormone, and increased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. The accompanying diagram highlights vitamin D metabolism. Which cellular change best explains the hypercalcemia?

options.text_html: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide
Unregulated extrarenal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in activated macrophages
Reduced osteoprotegerin production by osteoblasts
Failure of calcitonin release from thyroid parafollicular cells
Increased renal calcium reabsorption caused by autonomous aldosterone secretion

questions.explanation_html: Activated macrophages within sarcoid granulomas can express extrarenal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol outside normal renal feedback control. Increased calcitriol raises intestinal calcium absorption and can cause hypercalcemia with appropriately suppressed parathyroid hormone.

wrong_choice_explanations.5: Parathyroid hormone-related peptide can cause humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy, but the granulomatous disease pattern and elevated calcitriol indicate macrophage-mediated vitamin D activation.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Reduced osteoprotegerin can favor osteoclast activation, but it does not explain elevated calcitriol in granulomatous disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.1: Calcitonin deficiency is not a major cause of clinically significant hypercalcemia in adults.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Aldosterone primarily regulates sodium, potassium, and hydrogen handling and does not produce calcitriol-mediated hypercalcemia.

questions.educational_objective: Granulomatous macrophages can produce calcitriol through extrarenal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, causing parathyroid-hormone-independent hypercalcemia in sarcoidosis.

media.alt_text: Original schematic showing bilateral hilar adenopathy and macrophage conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol.

taxonomy.subtopic: VHL loss, HIF stabilization, and angiogenic signaling

questions.stem_html: A 58-year-old man with a long smoking history is evaluated for painless hematuria and new hypertension. Computed tomography shows an enhancing cortical mass in the left kidney. Hemoglobin is 18.1 g/dL. Histology demonstrates nests of cells with clear cytoplasm surrounded by a delicate vascular network, as represented in the accompanying schematic. Which molecular consequence is most likely present in this tumor?

options.text_html: Constitutive activation of RET after loss of extracellular ligand dependence
Failure of DNA mismatch repair with microsatellite instability
Stabilization of hypoxia-inducible factor with increased VEGF and erythropoietin transcription
Loss of RB-mediated restriction at the G1-to-S checkpoint
Activation of beta-catenin after APC loss

questions.explanation_html: Clear-cell renal cell carcinoma commonly involves loss or inactivation of VHL. The VHL protein is part of an E3 ubiquitin-ligase complex that targets hydroxylated hypoxia-inducible factor for degradation under normoxic conditions. VHL loss therefore stabilizes HIF, increasing transcription of angiogenic and oxygen-response genes such as VEGF and erythropoietin. This explains the prominent tumor vasculature and possible erythrocytosis.

wrong_choice_explanations.4: RET activation is associated with MEN2 and some papillary thyroid carcinomas, not the classic clear-cell RCC pathway.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Mismatch-repair deficiency produces microsatellite instability in Lynch-associated cancers and does not explain HIF-driven vascularity.
wrong_choice_explanations.1: RB loss promotes inappropriate G1-to-S progression but is not the characteristic molecular lesion in clear-cell RCC.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: APC loss activates beta-catenin in colorectal tumorigenesis and is not the defining pathway here.

questions.educational_objective: Loss of VHL in clear-cell renal cell carcinoma prevents HIF degradation, increasing VEGF and erythropoietin expression and producing a highly vascular tumor that may cause erythrocytosis.

media.alt_text: Original schematic of a vascular clear-cell renal tumor and the VHL-HIF-VEGF/erythropoietin pathway.

taxonomy.subtopic: Noncontact pivot injury and restraint of anterior tibial translation

questions.stem_html: A 19-year-old soccer player plants her right foot and rapidly changes direction. She hears a pop and develops immediate knee swelling. Examination several hours later shows increased anterior displacement of the tibia when the knee is flexed approximately 20 degrees. The accompanying sagittal knee schematic marks the injured structure. Which normal function has been lost?

options.text_html: Resistance to valgus stress at the medial joint line
Resistance to posterior displacement of the tibia relative to the femur
Stabilization of the lateral knee against varus stress
Limitation of anterior tibial translation and rotational instability
Conversion of quadriceps force into knee extension through the patella

questions.explanation_html: The mechanism, immediate hemarthrosis, and positive Lachman maneuver indicate anterior cruciate ligament rupture. The ACL runs from the anterior intercondylar tibia to the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle. It limits anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur and contributes to rotational stability during pivoting.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: The medial collateral ligament primarily resists valgus stress.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: The posterior cruciate ligament limits posterior displacement of the tibia and is classically injured by a dashboard mechanism.
wrong_choice_explanations.1: The lateral collateral ligament resists varus stress.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: The extensor mechanism depends on the quadriceps tendon, patella, and patellar tendon rather than the ACL.

questions.educational_objective: The anterior cruciate ligament restrains anterior tibial translation and rotational instability; a noncontact pivot with immediate hemarthrosis and a positive Lachman test strongly indicates ACL rupture.

media.alt_text: Original sagittal knee schematic showing the anterior cruciate ligament and the direction of abnormal anterior tibial translation after rupture.

taxonomy.subtopic: Functional asplenia, Howell-Jolly bodies, and encapsulated bacterial risk

questions.stem_html: An 8-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell disease is evaluated after recovery from pneumococcal bacteremia. A peripheral smear shows erythrocytes containing small, round, dark-purple nuclear remnants, illustrated in the accompanying schematic. Loss of which splenic function most directly accounts for this finding?

options.text_html: Production of thrombopoietin by splenic sinusoidal cells
Conjugation of bilirubin generated during erythrocyte breakdown
Synthesis of complement component C3
Maturation of neutrophil azurophilic granules
Macrophage-mediated pitting of erythrocyte inclusions and clearance of opsonized particles

questions.explanation_html: Repeated splenic vaso-occlusion in sickle cell disease causes progressive infarction and functional asplenia. The spleen normally removes nuclear remnants from circulating erythrocytes by pitting and helps clear opsonized encapsulated organisms. Howell-Jolly bodies therefore appear on the smear, and susceptibility to organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae increases.

wrong_choice_explanations.5: Thrombopoietin is produced mainly by the liver rather than splenic sinusoidal cells.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Complement proteins are synthesized mainly by the liver; functional asplenia primarily impairs filtration and immune responses to encapsulated organisms.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Neutrophil granule maturation occurs in the bone marrow and is unrelated to Howell-Jolly bodies.

questions.educational_objective: Functional asplenia in sickle cell disease causes Howell-Jolly bodies because splenic macrophages can no longer remove erythrocyte nuclear remnants; loss of splenic filtration also increases risk from encapsulated bacteria.

media.alt_text: Original peripheral-smear schematic showing a Howell-Jolly body and the normal splenic pitting function that is lost in functional asplenia.

questions.stem_html: A 36-year-old man has sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on the elbows and knees. Removal of scale produces pinpoint bleeding. The accompanying epidermal schematic shows acanthosis with elongated rete ridges and neutrophils in the stratum corneum. A biologic that interrupts the dominant inflammatory axis in this disease would most directly reduce signaling by which pathway?

options.text_html: IL-23-supported Th17 responses with downstream IL-17 activity
IL-4-driven class switching to IgE
TGF-beta-mediated fibroblast collagen deposition
Type I interferon activation of antiviral natural killer responses
C5a-mediated neutrophil chemotaxis from complement activation

questions.explanation_html: Psoriasis is driven by dendritic-cell and T-cell signaling involving the IL-23/Th17 axis. IL-17 promotes keratinocyte activation and proliferation and amplifies inflammatory recruitment, producing acanthosis, parakeratosis, and neutrophils within the stratum corneum. Therapies targeting IL-17 or IL-23 can therefore improve moderate-to-severe disease.

wrong_choice_explanations.5: IL-4 and IgE are central to type I hypersensitivity and atopic disease rather than the dominant psoriatic pathway.
wrong_choice_explanations.1: TGF-beta-driven fibrosis does not produce the characteristic hyperproliferative epidermal lesion.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Type I interferons are important in antiviral defense and some autoimmune states but are not the principal therapeutic axis illustrated here.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Complement-mediated chemotaxis is not the core cytokine pathway sustaining chronic plaque psoriasis.

questions.educational_objective: Psoriasis is sustained by the IL-23/Th17 axis; IL-17-driven keratinocyte activation produces acanthosis, parakeratosis, and neutrophilic scale.

media.alt_text: Original schematic of psoriatic epidermal histology linked to the IL-23/Th17/IL-17 inflammatory pathway.

taxonomy.subtopic: Asthma, eosinophilia, IgE, mucus plugging, and central bronchiectasis

questions.stem_html: A 29-year-old woman with asthma has recurrent episodes of wheezing, fever, and transient pulmonary opacities despite appropriate inhaler use. Laboratory studies show eosinophilia and markedly increased total IgE. The accompanying chest schematic shows central bronchiectasis with branching mucus impaction. Which mechanism best explains this condition?

options.text_html: Direct angioinvasion by septate hyphae during neutropenia
A Th2-predominant hypersensitivity response to Aspergillus colonizing the airways
Growth of a mobile fungal ball inside a preexisting lung cavity
Dissemination of yeast-filled macrophages from the lungs
Immune-complex vasculitis caused by circulating bacterial antigen

questions.explanation_html: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis occurs most often in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis. Airway colonization by Aspergillus triggers a strong Th2-associated hypersensitivity response with high IgE, eosinophilia, mucus plugging, fleeting infiltrates, and central bronchiectasis. The organism does not invade tissue in this allergic form.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Angioinvasive aspergillosis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients, especially those with prolonged neutropenia, and causes tissue infarction and hemorrhage.
wrong_choice_explanations.1: An aspergilloma is a fungus ball occupying a preexisting cavity, often after tuberculosis, and does not explain marked IgE elevation with central bronchiectasis.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Intracellular yeast-filled macrophages suggest histoplasmosis rather than Aspergillus hypersensitivity.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Immune-complex vasculitis does not produce the classic asthma, eosinophilia, mucus impaction, and central bronchiectasis pattern.

questions.educational_objective: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a noninvasive Th2-predominant hypersensitivity reaction to airway colonization in asthma or cystic fibrosis, producing high IgE, eosinophilia, mucus plugging, and central bronchiectasis.

media.alt_text: Original chest schematic showing central bronchiectasis and branching mucus plugging in allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

taxonomy.subtopic: Neutropenia, septate acute-angle hyphae, angioinvasion, and hemorrhagic infarction

questions.stem_html: A 46-year-old man develops persistent fever, pleuritic chest pain, and hemoptysis 12 days after induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia. His absolute neutrophil count is 90/mm3. Computed tomography shows a pulmonary nodule surrounded by ground-glass opacity. The accompanying tissue schematic shows septate hyphae branching at acute angles within a blood vessel. Which pathologic process most directly produces the surrounding radiographic opacity?

options.text_html: Mucus hypersecretion from an allergic Th2 response
Compression atelectasis from a freely mobile intracavitary fungus ball
Vascular invasion with hemorrhage and ischemic tissue necrosis
Caseating granuloma formation mediated by activated macrophages
Diffuse alveolar damage caused by bacterial endotoxin

questions.explanation_html: Invasive Aspergillus hyphae penetrate pulmonary vessels in profoundly immunocompromised patients. Angioinvasion causes thrombosis, ischemic necrosis, and hemorrhage around the infected nodule. On CT, this may create a surrounding ground-glass halo representing alveolar hemorrhage. Septate hyphae with acute-angle branching support Aspergillus.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: A Th2 response with mucus plugging describes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, a noninvasive syndrome.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: An aspergilloma occupies a preexisting cavity and can cause hemoptysis, but the neutropenia and vessel invasion indicate invasive disease.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Caseating granulomas are characteristic of infections such as tuberculosis and do not explain acute angioinvasion in neutropenia.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Bacterial endotoxin can contribute to sepsis and diffuse lung injury but does not produce acute-angle septate hyphae invading vessels.

questions.educational_objective: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in neutropenic patients is characterized by septate acute-angle branching hyphae that invade blood vessels, causing thrombosis, hemorrhage, and infarction.

media.alt_text: Original schematic showing a pulmonary nodule with a hemorrhagic halo and acute-angle septate Aspergillus hyphae invading a blood vessel.
